Basal metabolic rate in the Mountain mouse-warbler (Origma robusta) was assessed through respirometry trials conducted under controlled thermal conditions. At an ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], measurements recorded from post-absorptive, resting adults yielded a maximal oxygen consumption of 45.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 45.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value, reflecting the species' standard energetic requirements at thermoneutrality, is consistent with predictions for small-bodied passerines that forage actively in montane environments. The incubation temperature for eggs in this species is notably lower than the metabolic measurement temperature, with embryos developing at approximately 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Under these cooler incubation conditions, the age at birth, defined as the moment of hatching, is 14.5 days [ab = 14.5 days] at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This relatively brief incubation period aligns with the altricial developmental mode typical of many acanthizid warblers, wherein neonates emerge in a highly dependent state and require extensive parental provisioning during the early nestling phase.

The reproductive biology of the Mountain mouse-warbler exhibits a constrained seasonal pattern characteristic of highland species. Under the thermal regime typical of active metabolic periods, at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], females lay a single egg per clutch and produce two clutches per year, resulting in a maximum reproductive output of 2 eggs per year [Ri = 2 eggs per year]. This modest fecundity is balanced by extended parental care and a prolonged developmental schedule. The timing of first reproduction occurs at a considerable interval after hatching. At 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days], indicating that females defer their initial breeding attempt until their second calendar year. This delay likely reflects the time required for juveniles to acquire sufficient body condition and foraging proficiency to support the energetic demands of egg production and subsequent chick rearing in a resource-limited montane habitat.

Post-hatching development follows a clearly defined sequence of milestones in Origma robusta. At the thermoneutral temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the time since birth at fledging is 14.5 days [tx = 14.5 days], meaning that nestlings depart the nest approximately two weeks after hatching. This rapid transition from a sedentary nestling to a mobile fledgling is typical of small insectivorous passerines and minimizes the cumulative risk of nest predation. Gonadal maturation occurs considerably later in the developmental trajectory. At 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the time since birth at puberty is 43.5 days [tp = 43.5 days], indicating that young birds become reproductively capable only after they have completed the juvenile molt and attained a body size approaching that of adults. The notable gap between fledging and puberty, spanning nearly thirty days, represents a critical period during which fledglings refine their foraging skills and accumulate the somatic reserves necessary to support future reproductive effort.

Adult body mass in female Mountain mouse-warblers has been characterized through field studies of captured individuals. The ultimate wet weight for females, representing the asymptotic or maximum recorded body mass in adults, is 18.25 grams [Wwi = 18.25 grams]. This relatively modest mass is typical of acanthizid warblers, which are generally small-bodied and exhibit a streamlined morphology suited to active gleaning in dense understory vegetation. In contrast, the weight at birth, measured in newly hatched nestlings, is substantially lower at 1.8 grams [Wwb = 1.8 grams]. This pronounced disparity between neonatal and adult masses, a ratio of approximately one to ten, underscores the dramatic growth trajectory that altricial nestlings undergo during the brief nestling period. The species' comparatively small size at hatching may be an adaptive response to the energetic constraints of egg production, allowing females to allocate resources efficiently while maintaining a relatively short incubation period of 14.5 days at 36 °C [T = 36 °C].

Longevity records for the Mountain mouse-warbler indicate a comparatively extended lifespan for a passerine of its body size. Maximum lifespan in the wild has been estimated at 7.8 years [am = 7.8 years] when measured under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods at 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This notable longevity, equivalent to approximately 2,847 days, is unusual among small warblers and may be linked to the species' montane habitat, where harsh environmental conditions and reduced predation pressure in higher elevations can select for slower life-history strategies. The daily energetic cost of sustaining this extended lifespan is reflected in the species' basal oxygen consumption of 45.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 45.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a measurement that integrates both maintenance costs and the physiological demands of active foraging in a cool, high-altitude environment. These combined life-history traits underscore a strategy that prioritizes adult survival and repeated reproductive opportunities over a rapid, single-season turnover.
